record.original_question: Can one justify the numerically observed phenomenon that integrable point-vortex configurations are attractors for two-dimensional Euler flows with generic smooth initial vorticity and small numerical viscosity, and design a dissipation model for 2D Euler that yields such integrable large-time dynamics?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations on a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ (e.g., the plane, the torus $\mathbb{T}^2$, or a bounded simply connected region), written in vorticity form
$$\partial_t \omega + (u\cdot\nabla)\omega = 0,\qquad u = \nabla^\perp \Delta^{-1}\omega,$$
with smooth initial vorticity $\omega_0$. A point-vortex configuration is a singular vorticity field of the form $\omega(x,t)=\sum_{k=1}^N \Gamma_k\,\delta_{x_k(t)}$ with circulations $\Gamma_k\in\mathbb{R}$, whose centers evolve by the Helmholtz–Kirchhoff system
$$\dot x_k = \sum_{j\ne k} \Gamma_j\,\nabla^\perp G(x_k,x_j),$$
where $G$ is the Green's function of $-\Delta$ on $\Omega$. Such an $N$-vortex system is called integrable when it admits sufficiently many independent Poisson-commuting first integrals (in particular for $N\le 3$ on the plane, and for certain symmetric or constrained configurations for larger $N$).

Numerical simulations of the 2D Euler equations with small artificial viscosity, started from generic smooth initial vorticity, suggest that the long-time vorticity field organizes into a finite collection of concentrated vortex blobs whose centers asymptotically follow an integrable point-vortex evolution.

(a) Provide a rigorous justification of this phenomenon: prove that, in an appropriate scaling and asymptotic regime, solutions of the 2D Euler equations (or a vanishing-viscosity limit thereof) with generic smooth initial vorticity converge as $t\to\infty$ to configurations whose effective dynamics is governed by an integrable point-vortex system.

(b) Design a dissipative perturbation of the 2D Euler equations — i.e., a modification of the form $\partial_t\omega + (u\cdot\nabla)\omega = \mathcal{D}[\omega]$ for some dissipation operator $\mathcal{D}$ preserving the relevant geometric/Hamiltonian structure (such as Casimirs, momentum, or energy in a controlled way) — whose large-time dynamics provably reduces to that of an integrable finite-dimensional point-vortex system.
artifact.status_search_result: The literature shows active and ongoing research on point-vortex integrability, anomalous enstrophy dissipation, and long-time behavior of 2D Euler flows (e.g., Euler–Poincaré point-vortex models, vanishing-viscosity studies, recent work on point-vortex dynamics in $L^p$ vorticity classes). No source provides a rigorous justification that integrable point-vortex configurations are attractors for generic 2D Euler flows, nor a corresponding canonical dissipation model with provably integrable large-time dynamics. The problem appears open.

status_evidence.title: Integrability of Point-Vortex Dynamics via Symplectic Reduction: A Survey
status_evidence.snippet: Numerical results indicate that integrability of point-vortex dynamics is central for predicting long-time behaviour of 2D Euler solutions.
status_evidence.claim: The connection between point-vortex integrability and 2D Euler long-time dynamics is an active research direction without a complete proof.

status_evidence.title: Universality of the Anomalous Enstrophy Dissipation at the Collapse of Three Point Vortices on Euler–Poincaré Models
status_evidence.snippet: EP point-vortex system for N≤3 is integrable; as α→0 three point vortices converge to a self-similar collapsing orbit dissipating enstrophy.
status_evidence.claim: Dissipative regularizations of 2D Euler with integrable point-vortex limits are being explored but only in restricted regimes.

status_evidence.title: On the dynamics of point vortices for the 2D Euler equation with L^p vorticity
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work studies derivation of point-vortex dynamics from 2D Euler solutions.
status_evidence.claim: Rigorous derivation of point-vortex dynamics as attractors of generic 2D Euler flows is not established.
